topic.name: Adaptive Learning Systems
topic.description: Uncertain learner models, information value, and constrained adaptive assessment.

concepts.name: Probabilistic knowledge tracing
concepts.description: Maintaining uncertain learner-skill state from noisy, multi-skill response evidence over time.

concepts.name: Information gain
concepts.description: Expected reduction in uncertainty from an observation or intervention.

concepts.name: Adaptive assessment
concepts.description: Selecting questions sequentially to balance diagnosis, learning, coverage, and operational constraints.

misconceptions.name: One wrong response disproves every required skill
misconceptions.description: Deterministically marks all linked concepts unmastered despite slips and ambiguity in which skill caused failure.
misconceptions.remediation: Update a posterior through the response likelihood instead of assigning a hard state.

misconceptions.name: The highest-weight skill is the unique failure cause
misconceptions.description: Interprets content weights as a deterministic causal label for a multi-skill response.
misconceptions.remediation: Marginalize over plausible latent skill states and retain uncertainty about attribution.

misconceptions.name: Ambiguous multi-skill evidence is useless
misconceptions.description: Discards a response because it does not isolate one concept, rather than making a smaller joint posterior update.
misconceptions.remediation: Use a multi-skill observation model: ambiguous evidence can still shift several hypotheses probabilistically.

misconceptions.name: The hardest item is always most informative
misconceptions.description: Ignores the learner's current ability and the nearly deterministic response expected on an excessively hard item.
misconceptions.remediation: Plot expected information across item difficulty relative to the current learner posterior.

misconceptions.name: Mastery uncertainty is the only selection goal
misconceptions.description: Selects solely by a 0.5 mastery probability while ignoring item discrimination, prerequisites, learning value, and coverage.
misconceptions.remediation: Compute expected posterior change per candidate and add explicit pedagogical and content constraints.

misconceptions.name: Greedy information gain needs no constraints
misconceptions.description: Assumes repeatedly selecting one diagnostic item family is acceptable despite exposure, fatigue, coverage, and instructional goals.
misconceptions.remediation: Optimize information or learning value under content balancing and exposure constraints.

misconceptions.name: Information gain is the surprise of one outcome
misconceptions.description: Confuses the expected reduction in uncertainty before observing a result with the surprise of the particular result obtained.
misconceptions.remediation: Average posterior entropy over all possible outcomes before subtracting it from prior entropy.

misconceptions.name: Correlated evidence adds full independent information
misconceptions.description: Counts repeated or shared-family observations as independent reductions in uncertainty despite their common error source.
misconceptions.remediation: Condition the second observation on the first and measure only its remaining mutual information.

misconceptions.name: High outcome entropy guarantees useful information
misconceptions.description: Assumes an unpredictable measurement is informative about the target even when it is statistically independent noise.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare marginal outcome entropy with conditional entropy given the target hypothesis.

questions.stem: An MCQ requires both conditional-probability reasoning and calibration knowledge. A learner answers incorrectly. The item model includes nonzero slip and guess probabilities, and neither skill is known with certainty. Which learner-state update is most defensible?

options.text: Set mastery of both skills to zero, because an incorrect response proves all required components were absent.
options.rationale: The response could arise from one missing skill, both, or a slip; hard-zeroing both overstates the evidence.

options.text: Mark the highest-weight skill alone as unmastered, because a content weight identifies the unique cause of failure.
options.rationale: Concept weights describe item relevance, not observed causal attribution for this individual response.

options.text: Use Bayes' rule with the multi-skill response likelihood, retaining uncertainty over mastery, slips, guesses, and failure attribution.
options.rationale: A probabilistic observation model uses the response as noisy evidence and avoids pretending that a multi-skill item isolates one latent cause.

options.text: Leave both skill posteriors unchanged, because evidence involving more than one concept does not update either concept validly.
options.rationale: Ambiguity weakens attribution but does not make the response uninformative under a specified multi-skill likelihood.

questions.stem: An adaptive tutor has a posterior over a learner's concepts and a bank with calibrated item-response models. It must choose the next MCQ for both diagnosis and learning while avoiding repetition. Which policy is the strongest default?

options.text: Choose the bank's hardest item each time, because maximum difficulty produces maximum information for any learner.
options.rationale: An item far above the learner can yield an almost certain incorrect response and little discrimination among plausible learner states.

options.text: Choose any item whose concept mastery is closest to 0.5, without considering its response model, prerequisites, or instructional value during selection.
options.rationale: Posterior uncertainty matters, but an item can be weakly discriminating, premature, or pedagogically unhelpful.

options.text: Repeatedly choose the single item with greatest immediate information gain, with no content balancing or exposure limits.
options.rationale: Unconstrained greedy selection can overexpose an item family, neglect coverage, and harm engagement or learning.

options.text: Optimize expected information gain or learning value under prerequisite, coverage, exposure, diversity, and fatigue constraints, then update from the observed response.
options.rationale: This uses the learner posterior and item model while recognizing that a useful tutor has pedagogical and operational constraints beyond pure uncertainty reduction.

questions.stem: A hidden hypothesis H is equally likely to be red or blue. Test A reports H without error. Test B returns an independent fair coin unrelated to H. Before observing either result, which test has more expected information about H?

options.text: Test A: it reduces one bit of prior entropy to zero, while the independent fair result from B reduces none.
options.rationale: Information about H depends on uncertainty reduction conditional on the result, not unpredictability of the result alone.

options.text: Test B: its fair outcome has maximum entropy, so an unpredictable measurement carries the most information about H.
options.rationale: B has high marginal entropy but remains independent of H, making its mutual information with H zero.

options.text: They tie until one outcome is seen, because information gain is defined as the surprise of the realized result.
options.rationale: Expected information is computed before observation by averaging posterior uncertainty across possible results.

options.text: They add two bits together, because each binary observation contributes a full independent unit of information.
options.rationale: A binary outcome contributes information about H only through statistical dependence with H.

questions.stem: Two hypotheses have prior probabilities 0.5 and 0.5. A symmetric binary test reports the correct hypothesis with probability 0.75. Its two outcomes are equally likely. Approximately how much expected information does the test provide in bits?

options.text: About 0.415 bits, because the surprise of the less likely posterior hypothesis is the information gained.
options.rationale: Expected gain averages posterior entropy; it is not the self-information of one posterior branch.

options.text: About 0.189 bits, because the gain is 1 minus the binary entropy of probabilities 0.75 and 0.25.
options.rationale: Each outcome yields posterior probabilities 0.75 and 0.25, whose entropy is about 0.811 bits.

options.text: Exactly 1 bit, because an equally likely binary test result has one bit of outcome entropy.
options.rationale: Outcome entropy includes test noise; conditional uncertainty about the hypothesis remains after either result.

options.text: Exactly 0.75 bits, because each test contributes its accuracy as a full independent amount of evidence.
options.rationale: Accuracy is neither measured in bits nor additive without accounting for conditional dependence and uncertainty.

questions.stem: A second dashboard field is an exact cached copy of a diagnostic sensor already observed. The first reading changed the posterior over a fault. How much additional information about the fault does the copied field provide conditional on the first reading?

options.text: It provides the surprise value of the copied result again because realized information is counted per displayed observation.
options.rationale: Once the first field is known, the exact copy has no uncertainty and cannot change the posterior.

options.text: It provides high information because a sensor field with variable outcomes has high marginal entropy across incidents.
options.rationale: Marginal variability does not imply conditional information after the source reading is already observed.

options.text: It provides zero additional information because its value is determined by the first reading and leaves the posterior unchanged.
options.rationale: Conditional mutual information is zero for a deterministic duplicate of evidence already in the conditioning set.

options.text: It provides the same full gain as the first reading because separately displayed measurements count as independent evidence.
options.rationale: Presentation as a second field does not make a shared underlying observation independent.

questions.stem: An adaptive test estimates a learner near ability 0. It can choose among equally discriminating items with difficulties -3, 0, and 3. Guess and slip parameters are equal. Which item is the strongest diagnostic choice before applying content constraints?

options.text: The difficulty-3 item, because the hardest available response provides the largest information gain for any learner.
options.rationale: An item far above current ability produces a nearly predictable failure and little local discrimination.

options.text: Whichever item targets a concept with mastery probability closest to one half, without considering its response curve.
options.rationale: State uncertainty matters, but the observation model determines whether a candidate can reduce that uncertainty.

options.text: The highest-scoring item from one familiar family, even if repeated exposure and coverage constraints exclude it.
options.rationale: A local score does not override exposure, family independence, or content requirements.

options.text: The difficulty-0 item, because its response is least predetermined near the current ability and therefore most discriminating locally.
options.rationale: With equal slopes and asymptotes, information is greatest near the region where response probability changes most with ability.

questions.stem: A tutor's top information score belongs to a fourth paraphrase from a family the learner has already answered three times. A slightly lower-scoring item uses a fresh solution path and preserves later repair coverage. Which selection is better supported?

options.text: Choose the fresh-family item because dependence, exposure, and future repair capacity are hard constraints on useful evidence.
options.rationale: A constrained policy values independent evidence and preserves viable pedagogy rather than maximizing one myopic score.

options.text: Choose the paraphrase because the largest point estimate of information should override family dependence and coverage.
options.rationale: The score overstates useful evidence when repeated observations share a solution path and consume options needed later.

options.text: Choose the most difficult of the two because harder responses dominate selection quality after several exposures.
options.rationale: Difficulty contributes through its match to the learner and item curve, not as a monotone quality ranking.

options.text: Choose by mastery probability alone because uncertainty near one half settles the next-question decision without item context.
options.rationale: Candidate response behavior, independence, prerequisites, and instructional route remain material.

questions.stem: A learner has several strong, independent successes on one skill and then misses one moderately discriminating item. The observation model permits slips. What posterior response is most defensible?

options.text: Decrease mastery probability by an amount determined by the prior and response likelihood, while retaining uncertainty about a slip.
options.rationale: Bayesian evidence shifts rather than resets belief, and prior independent successes remain relevant.

options.text: Set the skill to unmastered because one wrong response proves the required knowledge is absent.
options.rationale: A nonzero slip probability makes the response compatible with a knowledgeable learner.

options.text: Assign failure to the highest-weight skill as the unique cause, independent of competing error explanations.
options.rationale: Content weights do not provide deterministic causal attribution for a noisy response.

options.text: Ignore the response because evidence with possible slips is ambiguous and therefore unusable for state estimation.
options.rationale: Noisy evidence can still update a posterior by a smaller, likelihood-weighted amount.

questions.stem: A debugging item requires both tensor-shape reasoning and backpropagation. A learner chooses a distractor consistent with a shape error, but the item is not perfectly diagnostic. How should a knowledge tracer use the response?

options.text: Mark both skills absent because an incorrect multi-skill response disproves all prerequisites used by the item.
options.rationale: The response has multiple possible causes and a noisy observation model, so deterministic failure labels overstate evidence.

options.text: Increase the shape-error hypothesis and modestly update linked skill beliefs according to the option and observation likelihoods.
options.rationale: The named distractor is informative but not conclusive; a probabilistic joint update preserves competing explanations.

options.text: Assign the miss to whichever skill has the largest item weight and leave other hypotheses unchanged.
options.rationale: A loading describes item relevance, not exclusive causal responsibility for one response.

options.text: Discard the attempt because evidence involving more than one skill provides no useful learner-state update.
options.rationale: Ambiguity reduces attribution strength but does not make the option-specific observation uninformative.

questions.stem: At the current decision point, an adaptive diagnostic converts every term to common utility points and scores continuation as expected entropy reduction minus a fatigue-and-reliability penalty minus response burden. Candidate H, the hardest item, scores 0.31 - 0.30 - 0.06. Candidate M, mapped to mastery nearest 0.50, scores 0.36 - 0.22 - 0.17. Candidate I, with the largest unconstrained information estimate, scores 0.48 - 0.34 - 0.18. Stopping now scores 0. Which current action maximizes the defined utility?

options.text: Stop the current diagnostic block because its utility of 0 exceeds H at -0.05, M at -0.03, and I at -0.04.
options.rationale: The stated sequential objective includes stopping as an action. All three continuation actions have negative current net utility; this conclusion makes no claim about a later rested or instructed state.

options.text: Administer H because the hardest available item is presumed to dominate easier alternatives even when its computed current utility is -0.05.
options.rationale: Difficulty alone does not determine information for this learner, and the supplied common-scale objective already assigns H less utility than stopping.

options.text: Administer M because mastery nearest 0.50 settles the choice even though its fatigue-adjusted current utility is -0.03.
options.rationale: A scalar mastery summary cannot override the specified observation reliability, burden, and stopping utility.

options.text: Administer I because its gross information term is largest and should override the penalties and the available stopping action.
options.rationale: Greedy use of the gross term discards the reliability and burden terms in the defined constrained objective; I's net value is -0.04.

provenance.derivation: H=-0.05, M=-0.03, I=-0.04, stop=0 under the utility function defined in the stem.

questions.stem: Define mastery as P(theta > 0). Learner A places probability 0.5 at theta = -0.1 and 0.5 at +0.1; learner B places probability 0.5 at -2 and 0.5 at +2, so both have mastery 0.50. For a candidate item, P(correct | theta) = sigmoid(theta), so both also predict a correct response with probability 0.50. A policy concludes that the item has equal information value for A and B. Which diagnosis is correct?

options.text: Replace the item with the bank's hardest one for both learners because a global difficulty ranking determines information across posterior shapes.
options.rationale: Information depends on the learner distribution and response curve, so globally maximal difficulty does not repair the collapsed posterior.

options.text: The equality is valid because mastery 0.50 is a sufficient learner-state summary once the two marginal response probabilities also match.
options.rationale: Both scalar summaries discard how strongly a response distinguishes the latent states inside each posterior.

options.text: Use the bank's largest stored one-step score while ignoring exposure, curriculum, fatigue, and later repair capacity because constraints do not justify a lower score.
options.rationale: A deployable policy cannot replace posterior-aware scoring with an unconstrained global ranking, and operational constraints remain part of selection value.

options.text: Compute I(theta; response) from each full posterior: it is about 0.002 bits for A but 0.473 bits for B, before applying operational constraints.
options.rationale: Both response marginals have one bit of entropy, but E[H(response | theta)] is about 0.998 for A and 0.527 for B. Equal predictive entropy therefore does not imply equal expected posterior entropy reduction.

provenance.derivation: For each symmetric two-point posterior, I(theta;R)=1-h(sigmoid(|theta|)); values are approximately 0.0018 and 0.4729 bits.

questions.stem: Four hypotheses A, B, C, and D are equally likely. Probe X reports whether the truth is in {A, B} or {C, D}; probe Z reports whether it is in {A, C} or {B, D}; probe Y returns an independent fair coin. Which two-probe plan has the greatest expected information?

options.text: Run X twice; each displayed binary result contributes a fresh bit even though the second result repeats the first partition.
options.rationale: Once X is known, its repeated value is determined and contributes zero conditional information about the remaining pair.

options.text: Run X and Y; both outcomes have one bit of marginal entropy, so together they resolve two bits about the hypothesis.
options.rationale: Y is unpredictable but independent of the hypothesis, so its outcome entropy does not reduce hypothesis uncertainty.

options.text: Run X and Z; their orthogonal deterministic partitions identify one of four hypotheses and reduce the two-bit prior entropy to zero.
options.rationale: X resolves one axis of the hypothesis space and Z resolves the other, producing two bits of target-relevant information.

options.text: Choose no plan prospectively; information is defined by the surprise of the particular outcomes after they have been observed.
options.rationale: Expected information is available before observation by averaging posterior entropy over the possible outcomes of a proposed plan.

questions.stem: After existing evidence E, a fault has posterior P(F = 1 | E) = 0.80. A second check Z shares part of the evidence pipeline, so its conditional table is used rather than an independence assumption: P(Z = 1 | F = 1, E) = 0.75 and P(Z = 1 | F = 0, E) = 0.25. Thus P(Z = 1 | E) = 0.65. Approximately what expected additional information I(F; Z | E) does Z provide?

options.text: About 0.622 bits, the surprise -log2(0.65) of seeing the more likely result Z = 1.
options.rationale: That number is the surprise of one possible realized output, not the prospective reduction in fault uncertainty averaged over both outputs.

options.text: About 0.123 bits, since H(Z | E) = h(0.65) is about 0.934 and H(Z | F, E) = h(0.75) is about 0.811.
options.rationale: Conditional mutual information is H(Z | E) - H(Z | F,E), so the supplied table yields approximately 0.934 - 0.811 = 0.123 bits.

options.text: About 0.934 bits, because the marginal entropy h(0.65) of the check's output is all information about the fault.
options.rationale: Most output entropy remains after conditioning on the fault and is therefore not target-relevant information.

options.text: About 0.722 bits, because another displayed check should eliminate all entropy h(0.80) remaining after E despite the shared pipeline.
options.rationale: A shared or noisy check is not automatically a full independent resolution; its incremental value must come from the conditional table.

questions.stem: A database-migration exercise requires transaction-boundary reasoning T and foreign-key ordering F. As a separate authoring annotation, its content mapping assigns weight 0.70 to T and 0.30 to F. Before the response, a tracer assigns independent mastery priors P(T) = P(F) = 0.70. Its wrong-answer likelihoods are 0.10 when both are mastered, 0.60 when T is mastered and F is unmastered, 0.70 when T is unmastered and F is mastered, and 0.90 when both are unmastered. After a wrong answer, which update follows from Bayes' rule?

options.text: Set both skills' unmastered probabilities to 1.00 because the wrong response disproves each skill required by the exercise.
options.rationale: The nonzero wrong-answer likelihood when both skills are mastered preserves posterior mass for a slip and for every joint state.

options.text: Choose T as the unique missing skill and leave F at its prior because T's higher 0.70 content weight identifies the dominant failure cause.
options.rationale: A content mapping weight describes authored coverage rather than a latent-cause observation. The supplied response likelihood table, not the content weight, drives the Bayes update for both skills.

options.text: Update P(T unmastered) to about 0.57 and P(F unmastered) to about 0.51 while retaining all four joint states.
options.rationale: The wrong-answer evidence has probability 0.403. The posterior numerators are 0.228 for T unmastered and 0.207 for F unmastered.

options.text: Leave both unmastered probabilities at 0.30 because a response involving two skills is too ambiguous to update either belief.
options.rationale: Ambiguity prevents deterministic attribution but the supplied likelihood ratios still update marginal and joint skill-state probabilities.

questions.stem: After a wrong response to a two-skill item, a joint tracer retains correlated uncertainty with P(A unmastered) = 0.30 and P(B unmastered) = 0.55. The original item had content weights A = 0.70 and B = 0.30. An A-only probe has P(correct | A mastered) = 0.65 and P(correct | A unmastered) = 0.35; a B-only probe has corresponding probabilities 0.90 and 0.10. The goal is to reduce failure-attribution uncertainty without making a hard mastery label. What is the strongest next step?

options.text: Retain the joint posterior, choose the B-specific probe because its likelihoods separate B states more strongly, and update from its response.
options.rationale: The B probe supplies about 0.526 expected bits about B versus about 0.056 for the A probe about A under the stated marginals, while preserving probabilistic attribution.

options.text: Mark A and B unmastered now and repeat the original item because one wrong response establishes that both required skills failed.
options.rationale: The joint tracer deliberately retains slip and alternative-state mass; a single response does not establish both skills are absent.

options.text: Choose the A-specific probe because the 0.70 content weight identifies A as the unique cause of the original failure.
options.rationale: A content mapping weight is not a causal observation, and A's available probe is substantially less discriminating in the supplied model.

options.text: Discard the original response and avoid either probe because uncertain multi-skill attribution does not support a defensible learner-state update.
options.rationale: Ambiguous evidence remains useful probabilistically, and a targeted follow-up can reduce rather than erase the remaining attribution uncertainty.

provenance.derivation: For the A probe, H(R)-H(R|A) is approximately h(0.56)-h(0.65)=0.056 bits. For B it is approximately h(0.46)-h(0.90)=0.526 bits.
